subsystems.name: Target identification
subsystems.role: Find molecular weaknesses that are unique to senescent cells and keep them alive.
parts: senescence markers such as p16 and p21

subsystems.name: Drug candidates
subsystems.role: The molecules designed or repurposed to selectively kill senescent cells.
parts: repurposed drugs originally developed for other conditions
prodrugs activated by enzymes enriched in senescent cells

subsystems.name: Delivery
subsystems.role: Get the drug to the tissues where senescent cells accumulate, while sparing healthy cells.

subsystems.name: Biomarkers and diagnostics
subsystems.role: Identify patients likely to benefit and measure whether the treatment is working.
parts: imaging of inflammation linked to senescent cells

subsystems.name: Manufacturing and quality control
subsystems.role: Produce a pure, stable drug that can be given safely at scale.
parts: biologic production for antibodies or peptides

subsystems.name: Clinical evaluation
subsystems.role: Test safety and efficacy in humans, then monitor long-term effects.

buildSteps.title: Map senescent cell survival networks
buildSteps.detail: Researchers compare senescent and healthy cells to find the proteins that senescent cells depend on to avoid apoptosis.

buildSteps.title: Screen compound libraries
buildSteps.detail: Thousands of molecules are tested on senescent cells to see which kill them selectively without harming normal cells.

buildSteps.title: Optimize lead compounds
buildSteps.detail: Medicinal chemists modify promising molecules to improve potency, selectivity and drug-like properties such as absorption and stability.

buildSteps.title: Test in cell and animal models
buildSteps.detail: Leads are tested in cultured cells and in aged or diseased mice to confirm they reduce senescent cell burden and improve health.

buildSteps.title: Evaluate safety and pharmacokinetics
buildSteps.detail: Studies measure how the drug is absorbed, distributed, metabolized and excreted, and check for toxicity in healthy animals.

buildSteps.title: Run biomarker-guided clinical trials
buildSteps.detail: Early human trials enroll patients with a specific disease, use biomarkers to confirm target engagement, and watch for side effects.

buildSteps.title: Scale up manufacturing
buildSteps.detail: Production is scaled to commercial volumes with strict quality control, and the drug is submitted for regulatory approval.

buildSteps.title: Monitor long-term effects
buildSteps.detail: After approval, registries track patients for years to detect any delayed risks of clearing senescent cells.

prerequisites.why: Understanding how senescent cells arise, persist and drive inflammation is the foundation for any therapy.
Most current senolytics also affect healthy cells, so true selectivity remains a major challenge.
There is no validated, minimally invasive test to measure senescent cell burden in patients.

prerequisites.tech: Animal models that mimic human aging
prerequisites.why: Mouse models capture some aspects of senescence but do not fully predict human responses.
It is not yet known whether removing senescent cells repeatedly over years is safe or has unintended consequences.

pathway.milestone: Early clinical trials in specific diseases such as diabetic kidney disease or Alzheimer's disease
pathway.unlocks: First evidence that senolytics can be safe and affect disease in humans.

pathway.milestone: Approval of a senolytic for one clear age-related condition
pathway.unlocks: A regulatory path and commercial incentive for broader development.

pathway.milestone: Combination regimens and use in multiple diseases
pathway.unlocks: More effective treatments by pairing senolytics with other therapies.

pathway.milestone: Intermittent or preventive senolytic therapy in healthy aging
pathway.unlocks: A new class of medicines aimed at delaying multiple age-related diseases at once, if safety is proven.
